narrative:
The model predicted an 84.8% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction to assess likely success in law school and beyond, your application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year class rankings had the strongest influence, both pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. You placed in the bottom decile for grades in both Year 1 and Year 3, far below the average of roughly the 6th decile among students who were accepted. These consistently low academic standings in law school were the main reasons the model saw high risk of bar exam failure.

Your LSAT score was the third most important factor, but it worked in the opposite direction. At 40, your score sits above the 37.2 average of accepted students, which helped reduce the predicted risk somewhat. However, this positive signal was not enough to overcome the much stronger negative impact of your class rankings.

Given these results, you should focus on strengthening your academic performance if you retake courses or consider programs that allow grade improvement. Raising your standing in law school classes would likely have the biggest effect on future predictions and improve your chances of admission and passing the bar.
